title: Cumulative smoking exposure and screening

cues.why: The screening task is legitimate, but 'Annual screening low-dose chest CT' and 'No scheduled screening chest imaging' explicitly repeat screening while the contrast-CT foil does not. This weakens that foil without selecting uniquely between the other two.

fairness: Offline editorial review only: no network or external clinical verification was performed; PASS does not confer clinical approval. All 18 after/candidate nodes were reviewed. Difficulty and high-yield ratings are qualitative judgments, not measured performance or verified exam-frequency claims.

Scope note: 4 rewritten and 14 new executable nodes were reviewed. The 12 retire-and-replace source records, the kept/held original question.n3.pleural-source-versus-systemic-response.v1, the unkeyed contaminated-pH idea and the additional parked/source-held topics were noted but not adjudicated. Only visible candidate presentation, update, exhibit, task, options, explanation and their sequence informed node judgments; author self-ratings and review-only key order were not evidence of quality. 12 + 0.5 x 22 = 23 pack-years. The named USPSTF framework, age, quit interval and asymptomatic presentation support annual LDCT among these choices. Willingness to pursue treatment is supplied; the explanation should not silently equate willingness with demonstrated medical fitness.

Calculating cumulative exposure and applying eligibility are two consequential operations, but the arithmetic is elementary and contrast-enhanced annual screening is a weak resident distractor. High-yield screening eligibility is tested at easy difficulty.
suggestions: Retain the source-specific task and cumulative-exposure calculation. Make the closest competing plan reflect a credible eligibility or screening-versus-diagnostic mistake, supported by a concise patient-specific observation.
If claiming ability to undergo curative treatment in feedback, supply the necessary clinical context or limit the wording to the stated willingness. Do not add unrelated difficulty.

title: Recurrence prevention after a first pneumothorax
fairness: Elective surgical consultation is defensible for a recovered primary spontaneous pneumothorax in an airline pilot concerned about recurrence. The explanation appropriately avoids implying flight clearance or mandatory surgery.

The occupation supplies the familiar exception directly. Identifying that exception and selecting its usual referral is essentially one-rule recall. Bedside chemical pleurodesis is poorly competitive in this young patient without a stated reason to avoid surgery.
High-yield recurrence-prevention counseling, but not a difficult two-step resident decision. No robust nonmedical wording-only method uniquely selects the key.
suggestions: Rebuild around a consequential distinction between plausible recurrence-prevention plans, with supported clinical findings that change their ranking; do not merely name an at-risk occupation.
Use specific comparable plans rather than a surgical assessment competing with an already selected bedside treatment. Keep the distinction between consultation, operation and occupational clearance.

title: Prevention after a contralateral pneumothorax
clarityIssues: The first node recommends a surgical assessment, but the later record never states whether an assessment or recurrence-prevention intervention occurred before the contralateral event.

cues.phrase: An at-risk occupation can justify offering elective thoracic-surgery consultation before recurrence.
cues.why: This earlier explanation rehearses the same referral chosen again in the later node. It does not prove the later answer, but permits answer persistence rather than a fresh comparison.

fairness: First contralateral pneumothorax supports elective surgical consideration even after leaving aviation. Low concern about recurrence is not an explicit refusal, so consultation remains a defensible best offered plan.

Interpreting the two-sided lifetime history and separating a recurrence indication from the obsolete occupational indication are real steps. The update changes the reason for the same action, however, and prior feedback lowers independent difficulty.

High-yield surgical indication. The later exhibit supplies both sides and the changed occupation, so it is interpretable with the shared presentation; the intervening treatment history remains unresolved.
suggestions: State the actual intervening care neutrally, so learners know whether this follows drainage alone or prior definitive intervention.

Test a different consequential planning decision after the later event, or give this objective a self-contained encounter without the preceding answer rehearsal. Do not label repetition of the same referral as hard.
Replace the weak bedside-pleurodesis foil with a clinically credible competing plan under explicitly supported circumstances.

fairness: Stable physiology, minimal symptoms, primary disease and follow-up support make conservative management defensible under the BTS approach described in the feedback. The 3 cm rim is not by itself proof that drainage is mandatory.

Guideline-specific differences in pneumothorax management are not resolved by the task; the feedback names BTS only after answering. This is an offline uncertainty, not a finding that observation is clinically wrong.
The preference and option structure collapse the intended size-versus-symptom reasoning to an easy match. High-yield management principle.

Clarify the intended guideline framework if it determines the ranking. Introduce a credible competing management consideration without manufacturing unsupported thresholds or removing safety findings.
Remove the founder narration.

title: Ultrasound localization for thoracentesis

fairness: Repeat ultrasound in the actual procedure position is the usual appropriate localization plan; the elevated hemidiaphragm reinforces why localization matters.

CT guidance is a potentially safe alternative, not intrinsically wrong. The explanation rejects the old mark but does not explain why CT guidance is less appropriate in this routine accessible-fluid setting.
This is high-yield procedural safety but essentially a single safety rule. The mechanical position mismatch does not establish two consequential clinical steps.

Make options parallel localization methods and explain why CT guidance adds no benefit for the particular accessible effusion. Do not imply that CT guidance is unsafe.

High-yield drain safety, but the stem effectively provides the malfunction and the distractors are mechanically weak: one consequential recognition step, not a difficult two-step problem.

IPC and talc pleurodesis are real downstream competitors. This is not merely a cautious option competing with arbitrary procedures: the record contains a specific unresolved symptom-attribution and expansion question.

The chronology is coherent and the imaging observations do not name the diagnosis outright. The post-drain air-fluid space should not be taught as universally diagnostic by itself; here the persistent separation and rind supply additional support.

Briefly include the established malignant-effusion result in this node's available current context so it stands alone without recall of an earlier exhibit.
Keep the prior feedback focused on the first decision; avoid adding the definitive IPC answer there.

title: Management of infection with a functioning IPC
fairness: Cloudy fluid, fever and S. aureus growth establish a clinical infection rather than an isolated positive culture. Continued free drainage, improvement on antibiotics and absence of tunnel/exit-site disease support retaining the catheter while treating.

Removal and exchange are credible foreign-body source-control errors. The observations distinguish this improving functioning device from one with failed drainage or persistent infection; no universal device-retention rule is asserted.

Similar option structure does not create convergence: all choices include antibiotics and the actual distinguishing action is retain/remove/exchange. No decisive nonmedical cue was found.

The later IPC placement follows coherently from the preceding plan. The current infection record is sufficiently complete to decide the catheter question, and previous feedback does not disclose this decision.

title: Mediastinal sampling before lung resection

cues.phrase: A bronchoscopic specimen has already established lung adenocarcinoma.
cues.why: The already-established primary diagnosis makes 'CT-guided biopsy of the lung lesion' an obvious repeat-of-completed-work foil. A nonmedical reader can eliminate it by chronology.

Distinguishing primary diagnosis from nodal staging and resolving potentially inflammatory PET uptake are consequential steps. Repeat PET after infection is a plausible tempting alternative, but the primary-biopsy foil sharply weakens the set.
High-yield lung-cancer staging. The known cancer label is necessary management context, not inappropriate diagnostic disclosure.
The explanation appropriately stops short of claiming a universal mandatory surgical-staging rule after negative endosonography, and does not leak the following pleural-dissemination result.

Remove duplicated accession narration unless it resolves a real uncertainty not already settled by the presentation.
Keep the recent infection and nodal findings; do not invent a mandatory post-negative staging rule to raise difficulty.

The malignant cytology is appropriate returned test evidence, not an authored stage label or management conclusion. Options are comparable treatment pathways and no decisive nonmedical cue was found.

The radiologist's unresolved differential is legitimate diagnostic uncertainty, not an answer label. Both MRI and PET options use 'characterization,' so wording overlap does not uniquely identify the key. No decisive nonmedical cue found.
The explanation does not identify the later operation. The subsequent solid-lesion result can follow coherently from the selected characterization.

title: Upfront resection of a localized thymic-bed lesion

cues.why: This pre-answer operability conclusion nearly restates 'Complete thymectomy with en bloc lesion resection.' It supplies both the interpretation and the procedure components.

The pre-answer surgical assessment already declares complete resectability. Selecting the matching operation is one rule applied to an authored conclusion, rather than two consequential interpretations. High-yield thymoma work-up but easy as written.

The later MRI finding resolves the earlier cystic-versus-solid uncertainty coherently. The current node supplies the necessary local anatomy and markers and stands with the shared presentation. Earlier feedback does not name the operation.

Supply enough supported observations for the resident to judge the biopsy-versus-upfront-resection distinction without declaring that judgment for them.
Use credible comparable procedural plans and explain the nearest wrong strategy; do not manufacture a tissue diagnosis from negative markers.

title: Initial tissue strategy for invasive nodal mediastinal disease
fairness: The invasive relationship, additional nodes and systemic symptoms make a histology-dependent process plausible and oppose treating this as a straightforward localized thymic lesion for immediate resection.

Core biopsy is a defensible best offered initial tissue strategy because architectural information matters in this differential. FNA is a real but less satisfactory initial-sampling alternative; the named parasternal route makes the core approach anatomically concrete.

Two consequential steps survive: interpret why imaging/location cannot justify upfront thymectomy, then choose a tissue acquisition method suitable for the differential. High-yield anterior mediastinal-mass evaluation.

The access statement permits both image-guided needle choices, so it does not uniquely enable the key. 'Solid tissue' is an anatomic target, not a diagnosis disclosure. No decisive wording-only cue found.

The explanation correctly avoids claiming normal germ-cell markers exclude all such tumors. A core sample is not guaranteed to settle every lymphoma diagnosis; the item asks for an initial plan and does not claim that guarantee.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between an initial core-biopsy plan and guaranteed definitive classification. Do not broaden the explanation into a universal claim that core biopsy always replaces further tissue acquisition.

title: Preoperative assessment of fatigable ocular and bulbar symptoms
fairness: The fatigable ocular/bulbar pattern in the thymic setting supports assessment for a neuromuscular-junction disorder, with respiratory muscle evaluation relevant to elective surgery. A normal oxygen saturation does not establish adequate muscle strength; the explanation is sound on that point.

The actual choice is between neurology, laryngology and cardiology. Classic syndrome recognition selects neurology; breathing-risk assessment is bundled into that answer rather than independently required to discriminate between plausible plans. High-yield thymoma/myasthenia association but easy, not two consequential steps.

No robust nonmedical wording-only answer shortcut was found: option lengths and referral-plus-test structures are broadly comparable. The weakness is clinical distractor plausibility and a bundled second step, rather than a demonstrable lexical leak.

Antibody testing is unnamed and 'breathing-strength tests' is imprecise compared with the standard's preference for actual named investigations. This does not make the current best offered referral unclear, but it weakens educational specificity.

Bulbar symptoms deserve clinical severity assessment; I cannot infer crisis from this stable fictional record, and the normal saturation must not be used to exclude respiratory weakness. No invented respiratory threshold is warranted.
suggestions: Replace unrelated specialty referrals with credible preoperative evaluation or sequencing plans that require interpreting the fatigability pattern and its implications for surgery.
Name the intended antibody and respiratory assessments after source verification, keeping option scope and specificity comparable.
Preserve the observed rest/use pattern and the warning that normal saturation is insufficient. If the aim is basic syndrome recognition, obtain explicit acceptance of that easier purpose.
